title: Read the Olive Oil Label
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Mediterranean Travels
description: A p5.js judging activity with nine illustrative olive oil labels: learners turn each label to read the back and judge whether it supports the claim on the front, using the EU acidity limits, the 27 °C rule for cold extraction, harvest dates, and origin wording.

learningObjectives: Judge whether each of nine olive oil labels supports the claim on its front, using the EU grade limits, the cold-extraction rule, harvest dates, and origin wording, judging at least 7 of 9 correctly on the first attempt.
prerequisites: The four grades and their free-acidity limits

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Judging claims against evidence with a visible standard, one scored attempt per label, and the deciding detail highlighted in feedback
keyQuestions: Does the bottle live up to its claim?
Which detail on the back label decides it?
Is this a marketing phrase with a legal rule behind it, or without one?
commonMisconceptions: Any oil called extra virgin is extra virgin, whatever its acidity.
"Cold" is a vague marketing word with no rule.
A blend containing virgin oil can be called extra virgin.
A best-before date in the future means the oil is fresh.
An oil bottled or sold in Greece is Greek oil.
assessmentOpportunities: First-attempt score on nine labels (mastery: 7 of 9).
Group the six unsupported labels by the kind of detail that decided them.
Judge the front claims of two real bottles in a shop.
